stage: as soon as detected during ANC visit
bodyEn:
Understanding Anemia
Simple Message: Low Hb(blood) may cause the mother and baby to be born weaker
Explain to the woman and family: During pregnancy, the body needs more blood and nutrition, If blood becomes low, the woman may feel weak, tired, dizzy, or breathless.
Actions to Promote: Go for all ANC check-ups at the health center, Get blood tests when advised, and Take iron tablets (लाल गोली) daily.
Family Counselling: Family members should: Ensure the woman takes iron tablets daily and Make sure she eats first or along with the family, not last.

Local Foods that Increase Blood
Key Message: Many locally available foodstuff available here can improve the Hb in your blood.
Iron-rich Local Foods: Green leafy vegetables (shepu, chaulai, ambadi, spinach), Ragi / nachni, Jowar and bajra, Roasted chana, Groundnuts, Jaggery (gur), Dates or raisins if available, Eggs or small fish (where commonly consumed)
Improve Iron Absorption: Add lemon, tamarind, or amla with meals.
Food Habit Advice: Avoid tea immediately before or after meals or after taking iron tablets.
Family Counselling: Families should: Ensure the woman gets extra portions of nutritious food and Not restrict nutritious foods due to pregnancy myths.

Taking Iron Tablets Regularly
Iron tablets help increase blood and prevent weakness during delivery.
Actions to Promote: Take one/two (as prescribed) iron tablet daily after food, If stomach upset or any other side effect occurs, inform ASHA/ANM/Arogya Sakhi and Continue tablets for the full course.
Family Counselling: Family members should: Remind the woman to take tablets regularly and Help her attend health centre visits for check-ups.

Danger Signs of Severe Anemia
Severe weakness, Difficulty breathing, Fainting or dizziness, Very pale palms or face and fast heartbeat (palpitations)
Action: Contact: AS/ASHA / ANM AT Nearest PHC or hospital, Arrange transport immediately.

stage: postpartum (PP1 or PP2 whichever is attended)
bodyEn:
Postpartum Counselling
Focus: Monitoring mother's Hb levels.
Key Messages: Due to bleeding post delivery, Hb may go down even further hence we have to be careful
Action: Report any instance of Severe weakness, Difficulty breathing, Fainting or dizziness, Very pale palms or face and fast heartbeat (palpitations) , Continue eating nutritious food, and Attend postnatal check-ups.
Infant Care: Breastfeeding is safe and encouraged.

stage: as soon as detected during ANC visit
bodyEn:
Understanding Pregnancy Nutrition
Nutrition is important for mother and the babay for its growth during pregnancy
If the mother does not gain enough weight, the baby may be born small or weak and this may hamper its intellectual growth
Actions to Promote: Eat frequently and add one extra meal to the day, Attend ANC visits regularly,
Family Counselling: Family should: Ensure the pregnant woman gets extra food during pregnancy, Avoid the practice of pregnant women eating last.

Local Foods for Healthy Weight Gain
Key Message: Many locally available foodstuff available here can help for healthy growth in weight.
Have food that gives Energy like Rice, Jowar, Bajra, Ragi / nachni, Makka; food with Protein like Dal (moong, tur), Chana, Groundnuts, Milk or curd (if available), Eggs or fish (where commonly eaten); nutritious and Protective Foods like Seasonal vegetables, Forest greens, Local fruits.; Ragi preparations, Jaggery, etc
Eating Practices: 3 meals and 1–2 small snacks daily and Eating even when appetite is low by having small meals

Rest and Workload
Key Message: Heavy physical labour during pregnancy can affect mother's strength and baby's growth.
Actions to Promote: Get 8 hours of sleep at night and Take adequate rest during the day. Drink adequate water
Dont: Avoid carrying heavy loads like firewood or water for long distances.
Family Counselling: Family members should: Reduce the woman's daily workload and Help with fetching water, firewood, and farm work.

Monitoring Mother and Baby's Growth
Key Message: Regular check-ups ensure both mother and baby are growing well.
Actions to Promote: Attend all ANC visits, Follow nutrition advice from ANM or doctor, Call AS/ASHA/ANM if she experiences: Poor appetite, Persistent vomiting, Extreme weakness

stage: as soon as detected during ANC visit
bodyEn:
Explaining Gestational Diabetes
When: After diagnosis of high blood sugar during pregnancy
1. Diabetes during pregnancy can affect both mother and baby, but it can be managed with proper care.
2. Regular ANC visits and blood sugar tests are important.
3. Following the doctor's advice helps keep both mother and baby safe.
Actions to Promote: Attend all scheduled antenatal check-ups, Complete recommended blood sugar tests, and Save contact numbers of doctor, ANM, ASHA, and nearest hospital.
Family Counselling: Encourage family members to: Support the woman in attending health check-ups and to help her follow medical advice.

Diet and Daily Routine
Focus: Blood sugar control through food and daily habits.
Eating the right foods helps control blood sugar and supports healthy fetal growth. : 3 main meals and 2–3 small snacks daily
To eat: Whole grains and millets, Pulses and protein foods, Green leafy vegetables, and Seasonal fruits in moderate amounts
To limit: Sweets and sugary drinks, Fried and packaged foods, and Excess refined flour and white rice
Family Counselling: Family should ensure timely meals and nutritious food for the pregnant woman.

Physical Activity and Rest
Key Messages: Light physical activity helps control blood sugar, 30 minutes of light activity daily (such as walking), if advised by a doctor, Avoid heavy work, Ensure adequate rest and sleep.
Family Counselling: Reduce the woman's workload at home and Support her in getting rest and regular meals..

Recognizing Danger Signs: Early care-seeking for complications.
Advise the woman to seek medical care immediately if she has: Severe headache or blurred vision, Excess sweating, dizziness, or trembling, Persistent vomiting or inability to eat, Reduced baby movements, Severe abdominal pain, Burning while passing urine, Fever
Action: Contact the AS, ASHA, ANM, MO or nearest hospital immediately.
Family Counselling: Family members should help arrange transport or ambulance quickly in emergencies.

Treatment and Monitoring: If given medication
Importance of following treatment plans.
Key Messages: Diet and exercise may control diabetes, but some women may need medicines or insulin, These treatments are safe and important for the baby's health.
Promote These Practices: Take medicines or insulin exactly as prescribed, Do repeat blood sugar tests when advised and Attend follow-up visits.

Delivery Planning
Focus: Safe institutional delivery.
Key Messages: Women with diabetes during pregnancy should deliver in a hospital with trained staff.
Action: Identify delivery hospital in advance, Keep emergency transport numbers ready, Prepare for possible early or cesarean delivery if advised by the doctor.

stage: postpartum (PP1 or PP2 whichever is attended)
bodyEn:
Postpartum Counselling
Focus: Monitoring mother's long-term health.
Key Messages: Diabetes during pregnancy may go away after delivery, but the risk of Type 2 diabetes remains higher.
Action: Get a blood sugar test 6 weeks after delivery, Continue healthy eating and physical activity and Attend postnatal check-ups.
Infant Care: Breastfeeding is safe and encouraged.

stage: as soon as detected during ANC visit
bodyEn:
Understanding Hypertension in Pregnancy
When: After diagnosis of high blood pressure during pregnancy
Key Messages:
High blood pressure during pregnancy can affect both mother and baby, but it can be managed with proper care.
Regular ANC visits and blood pressure monitoring are essential.
Early treatment reduces risks to mother and baby.
Actions to Promote: Attend all antenatal check-ups (ANC), Get blood pressure checked regularly, Follow all medical advice from doctor, ANM, or ASHA and Keep emergency contact numbers for doctor, health worker, and ambulance.
Family Counselling: Encourage family members to: Help the woman attend check-ups and Support her in following treatment and lifestyle advice.

Nutrition and Daily Routine
Focus: Healthy diet to manage blood pressure.
Key Messages: A balanced diet helps control blood pressure and supports healthy pregnancy.
Promote These Practices: Include Whole grains such as rice, millet, jowar, and ragi, Pulses like moong dal, chana dal, rajma, and peas, Green leafy vegetables, Fruits, Milk, curd, buttermilk, and paneer and Eggs, fish, or meat if part of the regular diet
Limit: Excess salt (about one small teaspoon per day), Pickles and packaged foods, Bakery items such as bread and biscuits, and Foods high in fat like excess butter or ghee
Family Counselling: Family should ensure the pregnant woman receives regular, nutritious meals and avoids high-salt foods.

stage: as soon as detected during ANC visit
bodyEn:
Physical Activity and Rest: Healthy lifestyle to reduce blood pressure risk.
Key Messages: Light physical activity and adequate rest help control blood pressure.
Promote These Practices:
Do 30–45 minutes of light activity daily, such as walking.
Avoid heavy work.
Ensure 8 hours of sleep at night and rest during the day.
Encourage sleeping on the left side, which improves blood flow to the baby.
Family Counselling: Family members should: Reduce the woman's physical workload and Support her in getting enough rest.

Treatment and Monitoring: Importance of adherence to treatment.
Key Messages: High blood pressure during pregnancy may require regular medication and monitoring.
Promote: Take blood pressure medicines exactly as prescribed, Do not skip or stop medicines without medical advice, Inform the doctor or ANM if there are side effects, Continue regular ANC visits and BP monitoring.
Family Counselling: Family should remind and support the woman in taking medicines regularly and attending check-ups.

Mental Well-being and Family Support
Focus: Reducing stress and encouraging care-seeking.
Key Messages: Stress can increase blood pressure and affect both mother and baby,
Promote These Practices: Encourage open communication with family members, Share worries with health workers or doctors and Practice relaxation activities such as light yoga or breathing exercises if advised.
Family Counselling: Family members should: Provide emotional support, Help reduce stress and workload and Encourage the woman to follow medical advice.

Recognizing Danger Signs: Early identification of complications.
Explain Danger Signs: Severe or persistent headache, Blurred vision or seeing spots, Difficulty breathing. Pain in the upper right side of the abdomen, Vaginal bleeding, Reduced or no baby movements, sudden swelling or sudden rise in blood pressure
Action: Seek immediate medical care and contact the doctor, ANM, or nearest hospital.
Family Counselling: Family members should be aware of these symptoms and help arrange immediate transport to the hospital.

Delivery Planning: Safe institutional delivery.
Key Messages: Women with high blood pressure during pregnancy should deliver in a hospital with trained staff.
Promote: Identify the delivery hospital in advance, Keep ambulance and hospital contact numbers ready, Avoid planning home delivery due to higher risk.
Family Counselling: Family members should:Arrange transport in advance and Support timely hospital admission when labour begins.

stage: postpartum (PP1 or PP2 whichever is attended)
bodyEn:
Postpartum Counselling: Continued monitoring after delivery.
Key Messages: Blood pressure may remain high even after delivery, so monitoring is still important.
Promote These Practices: Continue BP medicines if prescribed, Attend postnatal check-ups, Seek medical care if symptoms such as severe headache, swelling, or breathing difficulty appear.
Infant Care: Breastfeeding is usually safe, but mothers should consult the doctor if taking BP medicines.

Mental Well-being and Family Support
Focus: Reducing stress and encouraging care-seeking.
Key Messages: Stress can increase blood pressure and affect both mother and baby,
Promote These Practices: Encourage open communication with family members, Share worries with health workers or doctors and Practice relaxation activities such as light yoga or breathing exercises if advised.
Family Counselling: Family members should: Provide emotional support, Help reduce stress and workload and Encourage the woman to follow medical advice.

bodyEn:
Understanding High-Risk Pregnancy due to previous pregnancy complications
Key Message: If a woman had serious complications in a previous pregnancy, there is a higher chance that complications may occur again. However, with proper care and regular check-ups, many women have safe and healthy pregnancies.
Tell the woman and family: Because of previous pregnancy complications, extra care is needed this time, Regular check-ups help doctors detect problems early and prevent complications.
Actions to Promote: Attend all scheduled ANC check-ups, Follow the doctor's advice on medicines, tests, and diet and Stay in contact with ASHA, ANM, or doctor.
Family Counselling: Family members should: Ensure the woman never misses ANC visits and Support her in following medical advice.

Recognizing Danger Signs
Key Message: Women with previous complications should watch carefully for warning signs during pregnancy and seek medical care immediately if they appear.
Explain Danger Signs: Severe abdominal pain, Heavy vaginal bleeding, Water leaking from the vagina before labour, Reduced or no baby movement, High blood pressure(palpitations/breathelessness) with swelling of hands and feet, Sudden weakness or feeling very unwell
Action to Promote: Do not wait or try home remedies and Immediately go to the hospital or call for transport/ambulance.
Family Counselling: Family members should: Recognize these danger signs, call Arogyasakhi/ASHA/ANM in the area and Arrange immediate transport to a hospital

Managing Stress and Emotional Health
Key Message: Women who had complications earlier may feel fear, worry, or anxiety during the current pregnancy. This is common and can be managed with support.
Tell the woman and family: Stress during pregnancy is common, but sharing concerns and getting support helps reduce anxiety.
Actions to Promote: Encourage the woman to Share her feelings with husband, family members, or friends, Practice light relaxation, breathing exercises, or meditation if advised and Seek guidance from ASHA, ANM, or doctor when worried.
Family Counselling: Family members should: Listen to the woman and provide emotional support, Reduce her physical workload, Ensure she gets good nutrition and rest. Husbands should: Help with household work and childcare and Accompany the woman to ANC visits when possible.

bodyEn:
Preparing for Safe Delivery
Key Message: Women with previous complications should plan for delivery in a hospital with skilled doctors and emergency care.
Actions to Promote: Encourage families to: Decide the delivery hospital early, Keep hospital contact and ambulance numbers ready and Save money or arrange transport for delivery.
Explain that: The doctor may plan early delivery or a cesarean section if required, Delivering in a hospital ensures quick treatment if complications occur.
Family Counselling: Family members should: Ensure the woman reaches the hospital as soon as labour begins or if any danger signs appear.

Managing Stress and Emotional Health
Key Message: Women who had complications earlier may feel fear, worry, or anxiety during the current pregnancy. This is common and can be managed with support.
Tell the woman and family: Stress during pregnancy is common, but sharing concerns and getting support helps reduce anxiety.
Actions to Promote: Encourage the woman to Share her feelings with husband, family members, or friends, Practice light relaxation, breathing exercises, or meditation if advised and Seek guidance from ASHA, ANM, or doctor when worried.
Family Counselling: Family members should: Listen to the woman and provide emotional support, Reduce her physical workload, Ensure she gets good nutrition and rest. Husbands should: Help with household work and childcare and Accompany the woman to ANC visits when possible.

stage: postpartum (PP1 or PP2 whichever is attended)
bodyEn:
Postpartum Care
Key Message: Women who had complications earlier may also face health risks after delivery, so follow-up care is important.
Actions to Promote: Encourage the mother to: Attend all postnatal check-ups, Continue medicines prescribed by the doctor.
Seek care if she experiences: Heavy bleeding, Fever, Severe weakness, Pain or infection
Infant Care Message: Breastfeeding should start early unless the doctor advises otherwise. Ask the doctor if there are any concerns about medicines during breastfeeding.
Family Counselling: Family members should: Ensure the mother gets rest, good nutrition, and emotional support, Help her attend postnatal visits.

During pregnancy it is common to have some problems like nausea, vomiting, heartburn, constipation, or frequent urination. These usually improve with simple care.
Promote: Eat small meals many times a day, eat green vegetables and fibre-rich foods and Drink plenty of water or other fluids.
If you feel like vomiting in the morning, try eating dry foods like roti or bhakri after waking up.
Drinking cold milk may help during heartburn.
Not to do: avoid very oily or spicy foods
If you have burning while passing urine, fever, severe vomiting, severe lower abdominal pain, breathlessness, or extreme weakness, it may be a sign of illness such as infection or severe anemia. In such cases do not wait at home-contact the ASHA, ANM, or go to the nearest health centre immediately for treatment.
Action: Regular ANC check-ups, good food, rest, and early treatment of problems help keep both mother and baby safe and healthy.

Key Message: Every pregnant woman and her family should prepare in advance for delivery and possible emergencies. Planning ahead helps the mother reach a hospital on time and receive proper care, which keeps both the mother and baby safe.
Institutional Delivery: Delivering at a hospital or health facility (institutional delivery) is the safest option because trained doctors and nurses are available to manage complications such as heavy bleeding, difficult labour, or high blood pressure.
Encourage the pregnant woman and family to prepare the following before delivery:Choose place of delivery (Decide early which hospital or health centre the delivery will take place in), Know the nearest referral hospital in case of complications, Plan transport, Identify how the woman will reach the hospital when labour starts, Keep the AS/ ASHA/ANM/ambulance number or local transport option ready, Keep some money ready for emergencies, Identify a person who will accompany the woman to the hospital and stay with you;If the husband works outside the village, identify another trusted family member, Identify a relative or community member who could donate blood if needed, Keep contact numbers of ASHA, Arogya Sakhi, ANM, ambulance service, and the health facility easily available.
Government schemes: Inform the family about schemes that support maternal care: Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) – financial support for institutional delivery, Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK) – free delivery services, medicines, tests, diet, and transport in government facilities and Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY) – maternity benefit support during pregnancy.
Family Counselling on all the above.

stage: Show this for all the ANC visits
bodyEn:
Some symptoms during pregnancy can be warning signs of serious complications and should never be ignored.
If the pregnancy has been identified as high-risk, it means the mother may have a higher chance of complications. In such cases, regular check-ups and following the doctor's advice are very important to keep both the mother and baby safe.
Danger signs to look out for: Severe abdominal pain, Heavy bleeding or water leaking from the vagina, Severe headache or blurred vision, Swelling of face, hands, or feet with high blood pressure, Severe weakness, dizziness, or breathlessness, Fever, Burning sensation during urination and Baby's movements becoming very less or stopping
Action: Call AS/ASHA/ANM/doctor immediately and visit the nearest health facility.
Don't: Wait or try home remedies. Any delay in seeking care in these conditions can increase risks for the mother and the baby, while early treatment can prevent serious complications.
Family Counselling: Prepare which hospital you will go to if any danger sign appears, arrange for transport to reach the health facility and keep the contact numbers of AS/ASHA/ANM/Ambulance handy.

conditionLabel: Substance Use During Pregnancy (Alcohol, Tobacco, and Other Substances)
bodyEn:
Key Message: During pregnancy, the mother's body directly supports the baby's growth. Using substances like tobacco, alcohol, or other harmful products can seriously affect the health of both the mother and the unborn baby. These substances can lead to low birth weight, premature birth, poor growth of the baby, and complications during pregnancy and delivery.
Stopping the use of such substances as early as possible helps protect the baby's development and improves the chances of a healthy pregnancy.
Avoid alcohol, tobacco, gutkha, or any harmful substances completely during pregnancy.
Seek support from family members and health workers if she finds it difficult to stop.
Inform the ASHA, ANM, or doctor if she needs help to reduce or stop substance use.
If the woman is used to consuming such substances regularly, advise her to gradually reduce and stop with support, rather than continuing the habit.
Family Counselling Prompts: home environment should be free from smoking or tobacco use around the pregnant woman, family members should  encourage and help her stop using these substances and avoid using such substances around her, and help create a healthy and stress-free environment for the pregnancy.

conditionLabel: Micronutrient Supplementation and Preventive Care During Pregnancy
bodyEn:
Key Message: During pregnancy, the mother needs extra nutrients and preventive care to stay healthy and support the baby's growth. Taking iron–folic acid (IFA) tablets, calcium tablets, and recommended vaccinations and tests helps prevent complications such as anemia, weak bones, infections, and poor fetal growth.
Promote
Iron–Folic Acid (IFA) Tablets: Take one IFA tablet daily as advised by the doctor or ANM to prevent or treat anemia, Take the tablet after meals with water, preferably at the same time every day and Avoid tea or coffee immediately before or after taking the tablet, as it reduces iron absorption.
Managing Side Effects: Some women may feel nausea, constipation, or dark stools after taking IFA tablets. These are common and not harmful. If discomfort occurs, the tablet can be taken after food or at night. Drink plenty of water during the day. Eat fiber-rich foods such as leafy vegetables, fruits, and whole grains to prevent constipation. Include vitamin C foods like lemon, guava, or amla to help the body absorb iron better.Do not stop the tablets without consulting a health worker.
Calcium Tablets: Calcium tablets help strengthen the mother's bones and support the baby's bone development. Take calcium tablets as advised by the health provider, usually separately from IFA tablets. Continue taking them regularly throughout pregnancy as recommended for healthy growth of the baby.
Tetanus Vaccination (TD/Booster): Tetanus vaccination during pregnancy protects both the mother and newborn from serious infections. Pregnant women should receive the recommended TD injections during ANC visits.
Deworming: After the first trimester, a deworming tablet may be given by the doctor or ANM. Deworming helps improve nutrient absorption and reduce anemia.
Ultrasound: Ultrasound scans /anomaly scans help monitor the baby's growth and detect problems early.

After delivery, it is important for couples to plan and space the next pregnancy so that both the mother and baby remain healthy. Doctors recommend keeping at least a 3-year gap between two births. Proper spacing allows the mother's body to recover and reduces the risk of low birth weight, premature birth, and maternal health complications.
Couples can choose from different family planning methods available at government health facilities, such as condoms, oral contraceptive pills, Copper-T (IUCD), injectable contraception, or sterilization after completing the family. These services are available free of cost at government hospitals and health centres. Have a conversation woth your partner on these.
Discuss family planning options with the ASHA, ANM, or doctor, especially during the postnatal period or before resuming sexual activity. Planning together helps ensure healthy mothers, healthy babies, and better care for the family.

During pregnancy, the mother needs extra nutrition for her own health and the baby's growth. A pregnant woman should eat one extra meal every day and include a variety of foods in her diet.
Daily meals should include grains like rice, wheat, jowar, or ragi; pulses and dals; green leafy vegetables; fruits; milk or curd; and eggs or other protein foods if available. Foods such as groundnuts, jaggery, and seasonal vegetables are also nutritious and locally available.
Pregnant women should also take iron–folic acid and calcium tablets regularly as advised by the doctor or ANM, and drink plenty of fluids.
Families should support the pregnant woman by ensuring she gets adequate food, rest, and reduced physical workload. Good nutrition during pregnancy helps the baby grow well and reduces the risk of complications.

Breastfeeding should start within one hour after birth. The first yellow milk called colostrum is very important because it protects the baby from infections and helps build immunity.
For the first six months, the baby should receive only breast milk—no water, honey, ghutti, or other foods. The baby should be fed whenever hungry, usually 8–12 times in a day, including at night.
Breast milk provides all the nutrition the baby needs and also protects the baby from illnesses such as diarrhea and infections. Mother should have nutritious food and drink plenty of water that will aid in adequate milk generation.
Mothers should sit comfortably, hold the baby close, and ensure proper attachment to the breast during feeding. If the baby has difficulty feeding, the mother can seek support from ASHA, Arogya Sakhi, or ANM.
After six months, complementary foods should be started while continuing breastfeeding up to two years or beyond.
Family members should support the mother by allowing her time to breastfeed, ensuring good nutrition, and helping with household work so that the baby receives adequate feeding.

After birth, the baby needs immediate warmth and care. The baby should be placed skin-to-skin on the mother's chest, which keeps the baby warm and helps start breastfeeding early. The baby should not be bathed immediately; bathing should be delayed and the baby should be kept warm with clean, dry clothes. The umbilical cord should be kept clean and dry to prevent infection.
The baby should receive only mother's breast milk for the first six months. Do not give water, honey, ghutti, or any other food. Feed the baby frequently whenever the baby shows signs of hunger, such as crying, sucking movements, or searching for the breast. For small or low birth weight babies, frequent feeding and skin-to-skin care are especially important. If the baby cannot suck well, the mother can express breast milk and feed the baby with support.
Families should watch for danger signs in the newborn, such as:
Baby not feeding well, Fast or difficult breathing, Fever or very cold body, Yellow eyes or skin, Extreme sleepiness, convulsions, or continuous crying
If any of these signs appear, take the baby to the nearest health facility immediately.
It is also important that the newborn receives birth vaccines such as BCG, OPV, and Hepatitis B and continues with the full immunization schedule. Babies who are small or born early need regular follow-up visits.
Family members should wash hands before touching the baby, avoid harmful traditional practices, and limit visitors to protect the baby from infections. Proper newborn care and timely health care help ensure a healthy start to the baby's life.

During the first year of life, babies can sometimes fall sick quickly. Families should watch carefully for danger signs and seek care immediately if they appear.
Take the baby to the nearest health facility or contact AS/ASHA/ANM immediately if the baby has:
Poor feeding or refuses to feed, Fast or difficult breathing, Fever or very low body temperature, Yellowing of the eyes or skin, Extreme sleepiness or difficulty waking the baby, Convulsions or continuous crying and severe diarrhea.
These signs can indicate serious illness, and early treatment is very important. Families should not wait or try home remedies if these symptoms appear.

Vaccination is one of the most important ways to protect children from serious diseases such as tuberculosis, polio, measles, and hepatitis.
Every child should receive all vaccines according to the immunization schedule at the Anganwadi or health centre. Parents should keep the child's immunization card safely and bring it for every vaccination visit.
After vaccination, the baby may develop mild fever, slight swelling, or pain at the injection site. This is normal and usually settles in a day or two. The child can be breastfed normally and comforted.
If any vaccine dose is missed or delayed, parents should visit the nearest health centre and complete the vaccination as soon as possible. Completing the full schedule ensures better protection for the child.

stage: All INC visits between 6th and 10th month
bodyEn:
After six months of age, breast milk alone is not enough for the baby's growing needs. At this stage, the baby should start complementary foods while continuing breastfeeding.
Start with soft, mashed foods such as khichdi, mashed dal-rice, mashed vegetables, fruits, or ragi preparations. Food should be freshly prepared, soft, and easy for the baby to swallow.
Feed the baby 2–3 times a day at 6–8 months, and gradually increase the quantity and variety of foods as the baby grows.
Always wash hands before preparing and feeding food, and use clean utensils. Continue breastfeeding up to two years or beyond, along with regular complementary feeding.

Good nutrition in the first two years of life is very important for a child's growth, brain development, and immunity.
Parents should ensure the child receives: Regular breastfeeding, Nutritious complementary foods after six months, Growth monitoring at Anganwadi or health centre, Families should watch for signs such as:, Poor weight gain, Very thin arms or legs, Lack of energy or reduced activity, Frequent illness, These may be signs of malnutrition. If these are noticed, the child should be taken to the Anganwadi or health centre for assessment and counselling. Anganwadi will also support in providing food for the infant. Feed the child with it along with different nutiritous foods available.
Early attention to nutrition helps ensure the child grows strong and healthy.

Regular postnatal check-ups are very important, especially in the first few days. I will keep visiting you, but if you feel anything unusual, please don't wait-seek care immediately.
Please watch for danger signs like:Heavy bleeding, Fever, Severe stomach pain, Foul-smelling discharge, Breast pain with fever, Difficulty breathing or severe weakness. If you notice any of these, go to the hospital immediately or inform me.
Now, about your food—your body needs extra strength to recover and produce milk:
-Eat one extra meal daily and include protein like dal, eggs, milk, or meat (if you eat it)
-Eat iron-rich foods like green leafy vegetables, jaggery, and pulses
-Continue taking your iron and calcium tablets regularly. Take iron tablets for at least 3 months, especially if you had weakness or anemia
-Take lemon, amla, or other vitamin C foods to help your body absorb iron
-Avoid tea or coffee immediately after taking iron tablets
-Please also drink plenty of water and fluids.
For the baby:
Give only breastmilk, no water or anything else
Feed the baby frequently, at least 8–12 times a day
Make sure the baby is properly attached to avoid pain
You also need rest—try to sleep when the baby sleeps and avoid heavy work.
Your recovery is important for your baby's health, so please take care and ask your family for support.

Continue attending postnatal check-ups and stay alert for any danger signs like fever, heavy bleeding, or weakness. Even small problems should not be ignored.
Let's talk again about your nutrition:
Continue eating nutritious food with protein and iron
Take small, frequent meals if you feel tired
Keep taking your iron and calcium tablets regularly
Drink enough water to stay hydrated
Your family should ensure that you are getting proper food and rest.
For breastfeeding:
Continue only breastmilk for 6 months
If you have any pain, low milk concerns, or difficulty, please tell me—I can help
Now about your health and wellbeing:
Take proper rest and avoid overwork
Sometimes mothers feel sad, anxious, or stressed—if you feel like this often, please share with me or your family. Support is important.
family planning:
It is important to keep a gap of at least 2–3 years before the next pregnancy
There are safe methods you can use even now
You can discuss with me or at the health center to choose what is best for you
You are doing an important job caring for your baby. With good nutrition, rest, and support, you will stay healthy. I am here to support you—please reach out anytime.

stage: If the delivery outcome is 'Still birth' or 'Miscarriage' and 'Abortion' in Closure form
bodyEn:
Mental Health:
Pregnancy loss can affect your emotional health. Feeling sad or anxious is common- I am here to support you.
If you have persistent low mood, sleep problems, or difficulty in daily activities, let me know. Also talk to you rfamily member you feel comfortable with. Emotional recovery is important for future health.
Danger Signs (Seek Care Immediately)
Go to a health facility if you have heavy bleeding (more than 2 pads/hour), severe abdominal pain, fever, foul discharge, or dizziness.
Weakness or breathlessness may indicate complications. Contact me immediately.
Family Planning & Recovery
Allow your body to recover. Wait at least 6 months before planning the next pregnancy.
Use family planning to delay pregnancy until you are ready. I can help you choose a safe method.
Visit a health facility for a follow-up within 1–2 weeks and before planning your next pregnancy.

Drink plenty of fluids throughout the day—water, buttermilk, lemon water, coconut water, or dal water
Do not wait to feel thirsty—keep sipping fluids regularly
If you are breastfeeding, your body needs even more fluids
In hot weather or if you feel weak, increase your fluid intake
